tldr: When a robot performs long-horizon tasks, deciding "which past memory to retrieve" and "which past observation action deserves credit" are two major challenges. This paper proposes a theory and method unifying both problems through a single metric: the Value of Information.
overview:
When a robot repairs a home appliance, wiring details become invisible once the circuit board is removed. To plug a cable back into the correct terminal hundreds of steps later, it must recall just one wiring photo from a massive archive of past images. However, attending to all past frames at every step via full attention is far too expensive for real robots constrained by latency and battery life. An even harder challenge is assigning credit to the past observation action itself—recognizing that "looking over there in the first place was the right move" (O-CAP: Observation Credit Assignment Problem).

The authors realized that both "which memory to pull in (retrieval)" and "which observation action to reward (credit assignment)" can be explained by a single quantity: the Value of Information. They propose a model-based framework that leverages past behavioral history (rollouts) and a learned world model, deliberately masking parts of the history to measure the difference in predicted returns and estimate this value of information.

On the theoretical side, they demonstrate that reading the value of information at the observation provides a mathematically proven lower bound on the optimal Q-value of that acquiring action (flooring its TD target). As an application, they introduce "Memory Navigation," which uses a spatial pointer called "Memory Ghost" to traverse external memory. In MiniGrid environments, this allows the agent to solve tasks with high efficiency even when context length is drastically reduced.
contributions: Theoretically demonstrated that both memory retrieval and credit assignment for observation actions (O-CAP) are governed by a single quantity: the Value of Information.
Constructed a framework to estimate the marginal value of information without collecting separate trajectories, by intentionally masking portions of the history on a learned world model.
Derived a rigorous lower bound on the action-value function ($Q^*$) from the value of information, proving a theoretical floor that supports TD learning targets.
Implemented "Memory Navigation," navigating memory via a virtual pointer, and demonstrated that long-horizon memory tasks can be solved rapidly with a context of only 5 tokens.

sections.heading: Two hurdles for robots: Costly memory retrieval and crediting observation actions
sections.summary: For a robot to put past memories to use, it faces the computational cost of searching for the single relevant frame across its entire history, alongside the difficulty of crediting distant observation actions with reward. Both challenges can be solved in a unified way by knowing which information affects which decision—the Value of Information.
sections.details:
Imagine a robot replacing the control board of an unfamiliar home appliance. If it does not bring its camera close to observe the wiring before pulling connectors out, it will never see the original wiring again once the board is removed. Hundreds of steps later, the decision to plug a cable into the correct socket depends on just one frame among thousands taken in the past.

Two serious problems arise here.
The first is the cost of memory retrieval. Full attention over every stored frame at each step is too heavy for robots under strict latency and energy limits. Compression using recurrent states (RNNs) risks discarding information before decisions are made, while sparse retrieval from external memory fails to pass gradients to unselected memories.

The second is the Observation Credit Assignment Problem (O-CAP). When a retrieved memory pays off much later, how should the initial action of going to observe that cue be credited? Even Transformer-based reinforcement learning agents are known to fail on long-horizon tasks that require actively observing cues in advance.

The authors argue that both problems can be resolved through a single concept: the Value of Information (VoI, introduced by Howard). They propose an approach that estimates the value of information using archived rollouts and a learned world model, determining the retrieval set and assigning credit in TD learning at the same time.

sections.heading: Measuring and using the value of information: A theoretical floor and memory navigation
sections.summary: By deliberately masking history within a world model learned from past logs, the Value of Information can be estimated without running additional experiments. This estimate stabilizes learning by providing a strict lower bound (floor) on the TD target, while "Memory Navigation" traverses external memory with a pointer to enable memory retrieval with a dramatically smaller context.
sections.details:
### Estimating information value
In a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), the information $x$ needed at decision time $t$ may be acquired only rarely by an exploring agent. The authors train a world model $\hat{m}_\psi$ on the entire archived history. There is no need to collect separate trajectories with and without information $x$. By deliberately masking $x$ from the observed history, the model compares how achievable expected returns change with and without the information, estimating the marginal value of information $\Lambda_t$.

### Using the estimates and training
For action $a_{s-1}$ that acquired information at time $s$, an information credit $b_{s,t}$ computed backward from the decision at time $t$ is assigned. This formulation accounts for a redundant information set $R$ appearing after time $s$, ensuring credit goes to the earliest action that acquired the information.
Here lies the theoretical beauty: combining the return floor $L_{s,t}$ without the information and the information credit $b_{s,t}$ yields a theoretical lower bound (floor) on the action value $Q^*$. This floors the standard TD learning target, expected to accelerate convergence of the value function for distant observation actions.

### Memory Navigation
To reduce retrieval costs at decision time, the authors devised "Memory Navigation." In robotic environments, the set of memories needed at time $t$ often changes only slightly from the set needed at time $t-1$ (a local update).
Therefore, they introduced a persistent pointer called the "Memory Ghost." Just as the standard action head moves the robot within the environment, a second internal action head moves this Ghost across external memory space (indexed by when and where data was recorded). Only the memories reached by the Ghost enter the Transformer-XL context, keeping retrieval costs at a single layer regardless of total memory size.

After pre-training on MiniGrid-Memory-S9, testing on S17Random (with 5 tokens) showed that Memory Navigation achieved an average return of 0.95 in just 0.59M steps. This is noticeably faster than Gaussian absolute position retrieval (0.94M steps) and having no retrieval head (1.38M steps). Notably, the baseline without a retrieval head solved the task via a trick: varying its waiting steps depending on the cue type to force information into time embeddings.

sections.heading: Current limitations: Full implementation of theory and estimation error hurdles
sections.summary: Flooring TD targets using the value of information has not yet been fully implemented or verified empirically, remaining a theoretical hypothesis. Furthermore, prediction errors in the world model and upward bias from supremum operations raise concerns that the estimated lower bound might exceed the true Q-value.
sections.details:
The authors candidly acknowledge the following limitations:

- Incomplete empirical validation of theory: The information value estimators and the floored TD target itself have not yet been evaluated in a complete setup; claims of faster convergence currently remain theoretical hypotheses.
- Model errors and optimistic bias: The mathematical lower bound proof relies on exact ground-truth values. In practice, however, learned world models have errors, and taking the supremum over redundant sets $R$ and actions introduces an upward bias under noise. This creates a risk that the estimated floor exceeds the true optimal value $Q^*$.
- Policy dependence and history growth: Because the value of information is defined under an exploration policy $\mu$, policy versions must be managed as the archive updates. Moreover, while computational cost during inference drops dramatically, the training phase still requires the complete, uncompressed history.
- Information decomposition: When observations carry both redundancy and synergy simultaneously, the current formulation can only evaluate whichever component is larger.

sections.heading: Appendix: Why the value of information provides a strict lower bound on TD targets
sections.summary: Using Blackwell's theorem and the tower property of conditional expectation, the appendix rigorously proves that the value of information is always non-negative and establishes a mathematical lower bound (floor) on the value of acquiring actions.
sections.details:
The appendix develops the core mathematical proofs supporting the paper:

- Non-negativity of new information value (Appendix B): As a corollary of Blackwell's theorem in decision theory, expanding the available history set never decreases the achievable optimal expected return ($\Lambda_t \geq 0$).
- Bounded optimal TD targets for acquiring actions (Appendix C): For the optimal TD value of action $a_{s-1}$ at time $s$, the sum of a baseline $L_{s,t}$ (excluding observation $h_s$) and the discounted information credit $\gamma^{t-s+1} b_{s,t}$ at time $t$ provides a strict lower bound (floor).

The reason for splitting this into two terms is estimation efficiency. Directly estimating the entire floor requires backpropagating the effect of a rare $h_s$ across the long horizon from distant $t$ to $s$. In contrast, the baseline $L_{s,t}$ without information can be learned across all episodes, while the differential information credit $b_{s,t}$ only needs to be estimated near the rewarding decision time $t$. This separation provides a major computational advantage, dramatically speeding up early learning.

takeaways: Two major RL challenges—memory retrieval and credit assignment for observation actions—can be unified under a single metric: the Value of Information.
By deliberately masking history within a learned world model, the value of information can be estimated offline without collecting extra environment rollouts.

The value of information provides a mathematical floor on the optimal Q-value of an observation action, establishing a theoretical foundation to stabilize and accelerate TD learning for distant observations.

Avoiding full attention over entire memories and instead moving a pointer across spatial-temporal indices via "Memory Navigation" offers a promising way to achieve long- and short-term memory with surprisingly few tokens.
limitations: Flooring TD targets with the value of information remains a theoretical proof; full end-to-end implementation and validation on real hardware or large-scale environments is left for future work.
World model prediction errors and supremum operations in the equations carry a risk of overestimating the floor, potentially pushing it above the true Q-value.
Although inference compute is drastically reduced, training the world model offline still requires storing and processing the complete history.
